1.sense: The surah opens on the night, and the verb is left without an object. It covers, and the Arabic does not say what it covers, so the answer is the earth and whatever else the hearer is willing to put under it.

notes.t: Ghashiya is to cover a thing completely, the verb behind al-Ghashiyah, the Overwhelming. Night is described here as something done to the world rather than as a time of day that arrives on a schedule.

When Muadh made the prayer long on people, the Prophet ﷺ named the surahs an imam should lead with instead, and this was one of them. Its length was judged by him against the weakest person standing behind.
The present tense yaghsha sits beside a past tense in verse three. The night is kept as something still happening; the making of male and female is kept as something finished.

links.why: the same oath one surah earlier, with the object supplied
the surah after next swears by the night when it settles

2.sense: The matching oath. Tajalla is a verb of uncovering, the exact reverse of what the night was doing a line earlier, and between them the two verses take in the whole of a reader's experience of time.

notes.t: Tajalla is used of a thing that comes out from behind what was hiding it. Night covers and day uncovers, and the surah has taught its pattern of opposites before it applies the pattern to people in verse four.
The night is named first. That is the usual Qur'anic order and it matches an Arabian day, which begins at sunset rather than at dawn.
The Qur'an elsewhere calls the two of them two signs, and says the sign of the night was wiped out while the sign of the day was made visible.

links.why: night and day made two signs, one erased and one left visible
and by the day when it displays the sun

3.sense: The third oath is not by a thing overhead but by an act, or by the One who performs it, depending on how one small word is read. Either way it sets the making of the two sexes beside night and day as a third pair that divides.

notes.t: The grammarians read the ma two ways. As masdariyya it means by His creating of the male and the female, which swears by the act. As mawsula it means by the One who created them, which swears by the Maker.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both readings of the ma and the exegetes divide between them

notes.t: A reading transmitted from Ibn Masud and Abu ad-Darda recites the line simply as wa-dh-dhakari wa-l-untha. The exchange is recorded in the Sahih collections, but the reading is not part of the transmitted Mushaf and the community recites what is in front of it.
notes.src: the report of Alqamah with Abu ad-Darda in Bukhari and Muslim; the Mushaf carries the longer wording

notes.t: Three oaths, and every one of them is a pair set against itself. The verdict in verse four is about opposition too, so the oaths have already argued the case before the case is stated.

links.why: He created the two mates, the male and the female
and made from him the two mates, male and female

4.sense: The thing three oaths were sworn to establish. Human effort does not run one way. Shatta is a plural word for things that have gone off in different directions, and it is applied here to what people are spending their lives on.

notes.t: Say is not belief and not intention. It is running about and working at something, so the verse measures lives by their motion rather than by what they claim, and it addresses everyone at once in the plural.
Shatta is a plural adjective placed on a singular noun, your striving. Arabic does that to say the one activity has already broken into pieces, and the two pieces are named in the verses that follow.
The Qur'an states the other half of this elsewhere: a person gets nothing except what he strove for, so the scattering of effort is also the scattering of outcomes.

links.why: a person has nothing except what he strove for
whoever wants the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving it deserves

5.sense: The first of the two directions, and it is described by a hand and a caution rather than by a creed. He gave, and the verse does not say what or to whom, so nothing that counts as giving is left out.

notes.t: Ata is left without an object, which in Arabic makes the giving general. This is not a rule about a percentage of income; it is a description of which way a person's hand habitually moves.
Taqwa is added second so that giving is not left standing on its own. A person can be generous and still reckless with himself, and the verse does not let that half count as the whole.

The Prophet ﷺ recited these verses at a funeral in Baqi al-Gharqad, after telling the companions that each person is eased toward what he was made for, and they had asked whether they might then stop working and rely on what is written.
notes.src: Bukhari 1362 and Muslim 2647, the report of Ali ibn Abi Talib

links.why: those who spend their wealth by night and day, in secret and openly
guard yourselves as far as you can, and listen, and spend

6.sense: The third item, and the one that makes the first two something other than good manners. He held the best to be true. What the best is, the verse leaves as a definite noun with no explanation attached.

notes.t: What al-husna names is not settled. It is read as the reward, as the promise of the Garden, and as the word la ilaha illa Allah. The exegetes preserve all three and the verse survives each of them.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the reward, the Garden and the word of tawhid, and settles on none

notes.t: Saddaqa is not the same as believed. It is to declare something true, and its exact opposite, kadhdhaba, to declare it false, arrives in verse nine. The whole surah is built on that one pair of verbs.

Al-husna is a feminine superlative, the best. Whatever it names here, it is a promise that a person is either counting on or not, and the counting shows up in his hands long before it shows up in his speech.

links.why: for those who did well is the best, and more besides
and to each Allah has promised the best

7.sense: The return on the first direction is not a wage. It is more of the same road, made easier underfoot. What he was doing with effort he will find himself doing without it.

notes.t: The verb and the destination share a root, y-s-r. We will make it easy for him toward the easy. English needs two different words for what Arabic says with one, and the repetition is the sense.
The prefix sa- is the marker of the near future, not the distant one. The easing is not held back for the Hereafter. It begins in the next thing he is asked to do.
The Prophet ﷺ is told the same thing in nearly the same words in another surah, which shows the promise is not reserved for the exceptional.

links.why: and We will ease you toward the easy
those who strive for Us, We guide them to Our ways

8.sense: The second direction, matched item for item against the first. Where the other gave, this one held on; where the other guarded himself, this one decided there was nothing to guard against.

notes.t: Istaghna is a form meaning to consider oneself free of need. It is not the same as being rich. A poor man can hold this position and a wealthy man can fail to hold it, which is why the surah names the attitude and not the balance.
Bakhila and istaghna belong together in this order. Withholding is the act and self-sufficiency is the belief underneath it, so the verse gives the symptom first and the cause second.
The Qur'an names this exact posture as the reason a person overreaches: he transgresses when he sees himself as needing nobody.

links.why: man transgresses at the moment he sees himself beyond need
whoever is guarded from the greed of his own soul is the one who succeeds

9.sense: The exact reverse of verse six, placed in the same slot of the same sentence. He did not merely fail to believe the promise. He called it a lie, which takes work.

notes.t: Kadhdhaba is an intensive form and it requires effort. The surah is not describing a person who never heard the promise. It is describing one who heard it and pushed back against it.
The object is word for word the same as in verse six, al-husna, which keeps both men measured against one standard instead of each against his own account of himself.
This verb returns in verse sixteen as the first half of the definition of the wretched one, so the surah closes the loop it opens here.

links.why: rather, those who deny are busy calling it false
those who denied and called Our signs false

10.sense: The line most readers stop at. The same verb of easing is used, and it is pointed at hardship. Whatever he chose is made simple for him, including the choice that ruins him.

notes.t: To be eased toward difficulty is a contradiction in ordinary speech, in Arabic as much as in English. The verse keeps the word anyway so that the symmetry with verse seven is exact, and the strangeness is what the reader is meant to feel.
This is the moral shape of a habit. A refusal repeated often enough stops requiring a decision, and the verse describes that hardening as something done to a person and not only by him.
This pair of verses is what the Prophet ﷺ recited after saying that each person is eased toward what he was created for, which fixes the meaning of the easing to the road a person is already on.
notes.src: Bukhari 1362 and Muslim 2647, the report of Ali ibn Abi Talib

links.why: the one left astray finds his chest made tight and constricted
when they turned aside, Allah turned their hearts aside

11.sense: The one thing the second man was relying on is taken away at the single moment it was being saved for. The last word is a falling verb, and the picture is of a man going over an edge with his money still standing at the top.

notes.t: Taradda is from r-d-y, to fall from a height and by extension to be destroyed. Arabic uses it of a man who goes down into a pit and of an animal that falls to its death. Both senses are alive in the word here.
Yughni is the same root as istaghna in verse eight. He judged himself beyond need, and now the thing that gave him that judgement does not do the one job it was kept for.
The Qur'an says the same of wealth in several places, including of one man whose ruin it names outright.

links.why: his wealth did not avail him, nor what he earned
my wealth has not availed me, said too late

12.sense: After two roads and two destinations, a statement about whose responsibility the map is. The preposition is ala, upon, the preposition Arabic uses for a duty, and Allah places it on Himself.

notes.t: What is taken on is discussed. Most read it as showing the way, since Allah has undertaken to make the road plain to whoever wants it. Some read it of the reward that guidance leads to.
notes.src: at-Tabari prefers the showing of the way; the reading of the reward is also recorded

notes.t: Alayna is pulled in front of al-huda, and in Arabic that fronting means it is on Us and on no one else. A person cannot manufacture his own directions, however much effort he puts into the walking.
The same claim appears elsewhere as a flat statement: upon Allah is the pointing out of the way, and some of the roads lead elsewhere.

links.why: upon Allah is the direction of the way
you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides

13.sense: Both lives are named as property, and the later one is named first. Whatever a person thinks he is choosing between, he is choosing inside something that is already owned.

notes.t: The ordinary order is this life and then the next. Reversing it puts the Hereafter in the position of the more real of the two and leaves the present life trailing after it as an afterthought.

Both nouns are feminine adjectives with the word for life dropped out, al-akhirah and al-ula, the last and the first. Arabic can leave the noun unsaid when everyone knows it, and that makes the phrase sound like something already agreed rather than something being argued.
The identical phrase appears in another surah in the same order, so the wording is a fixed way of saying that neither end of a person's existence is his own.

links.why: to Allah belong the last and the first, word for word
to Him belongs praise in the first life and in the last

14.sense: The speaker steps into the first person and takes the position of a warner who has now done his part. The fire is left indefinite, a fire, which in Arabic makes it larger and stranger rather than smaller.

notes.t: The verb is in the past tense. The warning is treated as already delivered by the time the sentence ends, so whatever happens after it belongs to the hearer and not to the one who warned.
A canonical reading gives the fuller form of the verb with both letters, tatalazza, rather than the contracted talazza. The reading changes the weight of the word and nothing else.
notes.src: al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir reads tatalazza; Hafs and the majority read talazza with one ta

notes.t: Talazza describes a fire that has properly caught, all flame and no smoke. The Arabs used laza of a flame that leaps, and the Qur'an makes Laza a name of the Fire in another surah.

links.why: no indeed, it is Laza, from the same root
he will burn in a fire of flame

15.sense: A restriction, and it has troubled readers since the first generation, because taken flatly it would empty the Fire of everyone but the very worst. The next verse defines the term, which is how the surah answers the objection it has just raised.

notes.t: Two answers are given to the apparent restriction. One is that the fire meant is the particular blaze just described and not every punishment. The other is that al-ashqa here is a superlative in form without being comparative in force, so it means the wretched one rather than the worst of all.
notes.src: at-Tabari and the later exegetes record both replies without ruling one out

notes.t: Sala is to be roasted by a fire, to go into it and remain. It is a heavier verb than to burn, and the Qur'an keeps it for the punishment rather than for ordinary fire.
Arabic can use a superlative with no second party in view, the way the elder can simply mean an old man. Read that way the verse states who enters without ranking anybody.

links.why: the one who burns in the greatest fire, the same verb
the same superlative used of the wretched one of Thamud

16.sense: The definition of the term used one line earlier. Two acts, one of the tongue and one of the back. He said it was a lie and then he left, and the leaving is what makes the saying final.

notes.t: Tawalla is to turn one's back and go. It is the physical half of denial, and the Qur'an pairs the two verbs often enough that together they work as a single description of a person.
Naming him with a relative clause rather than a noun keeps the door open. He is not a category of person that somebody else belongs to. He is whoever does these two things.
The same pair of verbs describes the man in another surah who neither held the message true nor prayed, but denied and turned away.

links.why: but he denied and turned away
have you seen if he denied and turned away

words.g: and he will be kept away from it

17.sense: The matching promise. He is not described as escaping the fire. He is described as having it steered away from him, which puts the effort on somebody else's side of the ledger.

notes.t: Jannaba is to set a thing off to one side, away from the flank. The passive here means the man does not have to do the steering; he is steered, and he learns about it afterwards.
Al-atqa answers al-ashqa exactly, superlative for superlative, and the two words rhyme in Arabic. The surah is arranging its two men as mirror images down to the sound of their names.
The same verb appears in another short surah with the roles reversed, where it is the wretched one who keeps himself away from the reminder.

links.why: the same verb of being set aside, there of the wretched turning from the reminder
then We deliver those who guarded themselves and leave the wrongdoers

18.sense: The definition of the second man, and this time the thing given is named. Not a surplus and not a portion described as small, but his wealth, and the clause at the end says the giving is done to clean the giver rather than to relieve the receiver.

notes.t: Zakah and tazkiyah come from a root that means both to purify and to grow. Arabic does not separate the two, so the wealth going out and the man being made larger are one motion inside a single word.

Many early authorities read these closing verses in the light of Abu Bakr, who bought tortured slaves out of their owners' hands and asked nothing back from them. The reading is old and widely held, and the reports carrying it are discussed rather than agreed.
notes.src: Ibn Kathir and others record the reports naming Abu Bakr; their chains and gradings are discussed

notes.t: The Qur'an gives the same purpose for the charity taken from wealth, that it purifies the people it is taken from, so the motive here is not an unusual one.

links.why: take a charity from their wealth, purifying them by it
he has succeeded who purified himself

19.sense: The giving is stripped of the one motive that would explain it in ordinary terms. Nobody has done him a favour that he is now settling. He is not paying anyone back, which removes the last account the transaction could have belonged to.

notes.t: This is the ordinary social economy of the Arabs and of everybody else. Gifts create obligations and obligations get discharged, usually in public. The verse lifts the praised giver out of that system entirely.
The negation uses min before nimatin, which makes it total. Not a small favour, not a favour long ago, not any favour of any size at all.
The Qur'an puts the same disclaimer in the mouths of others who feed the poor and say plainly that they want no repayment and no thanks.

links.why: we feed you for the face of Allah, wanting no reward and no thanks
do not cancel your charity by reminding people of it

20.sense: The one motive left standing after the others are ruled out. Everything he did has a single address, and the verse names it with the highest of the descriptions available to it.

notes.t: The grammarians call this exception munqati, a break rather than a carve-out. Seeking the face of his Lord is not one more item on the list of debts being settled. It is a different kind of thing from everything the list contained.

What is meant by the face of Allah is discussed at length by the exegetes and the schools of creed. The position of the early generations is to affirm what He affirmed of Himself without likening it to anything created and without denying it.
notes.src: the schools of creed differ on the wajh; the position reported from the early generations is affirmation without likeness

notes.t: Al-ala, the Most High, attaches to his Lord and not to the face. Putting it at the very end of the sentence lets the surah climb one last step before its closing verse.

links.why: that is better for those who want the face of Allah
those who call on their Lord morning and evening, wanting His face

21.sense: Two words end the surah. He is not promised his wealth back, or safety, or a name people remember. He is promised the state the man in verse eight was trying to buy and did not get.

notes.t: Sawfa is the particle of the far future and the lam in front of it is emphasis. Together they say the thing is certain and it is not yet, which is exactly the position the giver was already living in while he gave.
The verb has no object. He will be satisfied, and the verse does not say with what, so nothing is left outside the satisfaction and nothing has to be listed.
The Prophet ﷺ is given the same promise in nearly the same words two surahs later, with the same particle of the far future in front of it.

links.why: your Lord will give you, and you will be satisfied
return to your Lord, well pleased and pleasing to Him
